title: British European Airways Flight 548

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: Report on the accident to Hawker Siddeley Trident 1C G-ARPI near Staines-upon-Thames, Surrey on 18 June 1972

summary: Hawker Siddeley Trident 1C G-ARPI crashed shortly after takeoff from Heathrow near Staines-upon-Thames. During the initial climb in noise-abatement configuration, the aircraft lost airspeed and the captain unintentionally retracted the leading edge droops at an insufficient airspeed of 162 knots (20 knots below minimum). The aircraft entered a deep stall from which recovery was impossible at the low altitude.
probable_cause: The captain failed to maintain adequate airspeed during climb and failed to extend the leading edge droops properly. Contributing factors included the captain's undiagnosed heart condition, limited co-pilot experience, an aircraft design vulnerable to deep stall if droops were retracted at low speed, and inadequate stall recovery system training.

factors.evidence: Captain failed to maintain airspeed above 177 knots and retracted droops at 162 knots, 20 knots below minimum speed (p. 531-544).
Captain Key had an undiagnosed heart condition that may have impaired judgment (p. 26-30).
Second officer Keighley had limited experience and was not qualified to act as pilot-flying for the aircraft (p. 37-42).
Trident T-tail design with retractable droops made it vulnerable to deep stall if droops retracted below minimum speed (p. 660-679).
Aircraft entered deep stall at second 116 after droop retraction, with stick-pusher system providing insufficient warning (p. 497-507).
Aircraft descended steeply after deep stall with no recovery possible at 1772 feet altitude (p. 506-507).
Aircraft impacted ground near Staines-upon-Thames at second 150.7 (p. 508).

events.text: Brake release, start of takeoff roll on runway 28R.
Aircraft rotates at 145 knots IAS, leaves runway 2 seconds later (p. 471-472).
Autopilot engaged at 355 feet above runway, airspeed 170 knots IAS, 7 knots below noise-abatement target (p. 472-473).
Aircraft begins 20-degree banked turn to port towards Epsom NDB (p. 474-475).
Captain reports 'Climbing as cleared', instructed to contact London ATC on 128.4 MHz (p. 476-477).
Noise-abatement procedure initiated: flaps retracted to fully up, power reduced. Airspeed 168 knots, still 9 knots below target (p. 487-489).
After thrust reduction, airspeed drops to 157 knots, 20 knots below noise-abatement target Vy of 177 knots (p. 540-541).
Droop lever selected up in 20-degree banked turn at 162 knots IAS, 1772 feet altitude, 20 knots below droop retraction minimum (p. 496-498, 543-544).
Stick-pusher stall recovery device operates at low airspeed, autopilot automatically disengages, nose pitches down (p. 498-500).
Second stick-push operates as elevator trim configuration causes pitch-up after first pitch-down (p. 503).
Stall recovery system manually inhibited by pulling override lever. Aircraft pitched up rapidly, lost speed and height (p. 504-506).
Aircraft impacted field near Staines-upon-Thames, all 118 occupants killed (p. 508).

recommendations.text: Speed-operated baulk to prevent retraction of leading-edge droops or slats when airspeed is below safe limit.

Specific instruction and training on change of configuration stalls, simultaneous stick-shaker/stick-pusher operation, and implications of design differences between stick-shaker and stick-pusher mechanisms (p. 3013-3023).
Mandatory carriage of cockpit voice recorders on all civil passenger-carrying aircraft over 27,000 kg all-up weight (p. 3026-3028).
Pilot training on possibility and dangers of subtle pilot incapacitation (p. 3030-3031).
Young trainee pilots given more experience on flight deck before operating as P2 on passenger flights (p. 3033-3039).
Substitute stress-test electrocardiogram for resting ECG in pilot medicals when reliability improves (p. 3041-3043).
P4 seat occupied only by personnel with flight function or under training during critical flight phases (p. 3045-3047).

safety_changes: Cockpit voice recorders became mandatory on large aircraft
